Idle
ī´dl
adj. (unemployed, empty; rendering Greek argos)
Old English idel, empty, vain. The Greek argos is a contraction of a-ergos, without work — idleness is a vacancy, not a rest.

Biblical Definition

Idle means empty of useful work. Christ attaches judgment to idle speech: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Mat 12:36) — the emptiness itself is the charge. The householder finds men standing idle in the marketplace and sends them into the vineyard even at the eleventh hour (Mat 20:6). Paul warns Timothy that idleness in young widows breeds more than inactivity: they “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies” (1Ti 5:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines idle as not employed; unoccupied with business; unemployed; and as useless, vain, ineffectual, of no importance.

expand to see more

IDLE, a. Not employed; unoccupied with business; unemployed; applied to persons.

2. Unemployed; vacant; applied to time.

3. Useless; vain; ineffectual.

4. Trifling; vain; of no importance; as idle talk.

Key Scripture

Mat 12:36 — "But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment."

Mat 20:6 — "And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and saith unto them, Why stand ye here all the day idle?"

1Ti 5:13 — "And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not."

Pro 19:15 — "Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger."

Modern Corruption

Idleness is now impossible to see, because constant activity conceals it — a person can be occupied every waking hour and still be, in the biblical sense, doing nothing.

expand to see more

1 Timothy 5:13 traces a progression the church would recognize if it looked: they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. Idleness does not stay empty. A life with no assigned work does not remain neutral; it fills with other people's business, and the tongue supplies the occupation the hands lack. That is why Paul's remedy is not merely rest but employment.

Matthew 12:36 is the verse that unsettles everyone who reads it slowly. Not every wicked word — every idle word. The standard is not malice but emptiness, speech that carried nothing and cost nothing and was therefore assumed to be free. Christ's point is not to make His hearers mute but to show that nothing is unweighed, and that the cure is a good treasure in the heart, out of which the mouth speaks.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek argos (G692), inactive, unemployed, barren; Hebrew atsel (H6101), sluggish — the sluggard of Proverbs.

expand to see more

Greek argos (G692) — idle, unproductive; Matthew 12:36, 20:3-6, 1 Timothy 5:13, Titus 1:12.

Hebrew atslah (H6103) — idleness, slothfulness; Proverbs 19:15, 31:27, she eateth not the bread of idleness.

Greek ataktos (G813) — disorderly; 2 Thessalonians 3:11, working not at all, but are busybodies.

Usage

"“Every idle word… they shall give account thereof” — emptiness is the charge."

"“Why stand ye here all the day idle?” — the eleventh-hour call to the vineyard."

"“Not only idle, but tattlers also” — idleness never stays empty."
